item.content:encoded: A sharp sell-off in [USN:L1N45N082 TEXT:"European government bonds"] this month shows how hedge funds' growing role is making a systemically important market more vulnerable — a risk regulators are watching closely. On the surface, the [USN:L1N44U082 TEXT:"reasons for"] a surge in French 10-year yields to 24-year highs were clear: a growing [USN:L8N45U1VY TEXT:"government debt"] burden, inflation fanned by high energy costs, and competition for capital from a global data-centre boom that is lifting economic growth. But some investors said the scale and speed of the moves showed hedge funds were fuelling volatility in the market as they rapidly unwound trades. No obvious trigger preceded the unusually large daily yield increases of over 10 basis points (bps) and nearly 25 bp two-day jump in the premium investors demand to hold French debt over German bonds, the most since the euro zone debt crisis. Yields rise as bond prices fall. , . The European Central Bank estimates that hedge funds account for more than half of trading in the roughly $13 trillion European government bond market, up from 30% in 2020. The International Monetary Fund says hedge fund exposure to sovereign bonds has more than doubled since 2022, without giving a total. "The hedge fund community has ballooned," said Lauréline Renaud-Chatelain, fixed income strategy lead at Pictet Wealth Management. "It's bringing a lot more volatility to the bond market and potentially explains why the (French) sell-off was severe in a context where we lacked a real catalyst." HEDGE FUNDS CAN AMPLIFY PRICE MOVES Hedge funds oversee over $40 trillion, including the borrowed funds they use to leverage their bets and exposure through derivatives, according to the IMF. They rarely share details of their investments and will bet on asset prices falling as well as rising. Their role in sovereign debt trading matters because it impacts governments' funding, which in turn can affect borrowing costs for companies and homeowners. Increased hedge fund trading activity can "amplify price dislocations and liquidity strains during periods of stress," the IMF said in October. It cited hedge funds' borrowing and crowded trades, in which many funds hold similar positions. The European Securities and Markets Authority, the region's financial watchdog, declined to comment for this story. Certain strategies popular with hedge funds are sensitive to price and volatility changes, said Bruno Schneller, managing partner at Erlen Capital Management, which invests in hedge funds. These include cash-futures [USN:L1N45E0NO TEXT:"basis trades"] and leveraged carry trades. In a basis trade, hedge funds seek to profit from the narrow price difference between bond securities and futures. A carry trade involves borrowing cash in a currency with low interest rates to bet on other assets. When things change, "investors may need to reduce exposure relatively quickly ... creating the potential for market moves to become self-reinforcing," said Schneller. But he cautioned against attributing the recent volatility solely to hedge funds given fundamental drivers, notably in France. Political jostling ahead of 2027's presidential election could hinder efforts to reduce France's high deficit, one factor which has rattled markets. HEDGE FUNDS STEP IN AS OTHER INVESTORS DRAW BACK Jiri Krol, global head of government affairs at the Alternative Investment Management Association, a private markets industry group, said hedge funds were one of bond markets' most important sources of liquidity. "As for recent market dynamics, we caution against hasty, broadbrush pronouncements based on anecdotal evidence about the role of particular categories of market participant," he said. Hedge funds have taken a greater share of government bond markets as other buyers retreat. Central banks are shrinking balance sheets, changes in pension schemes are reducing demand for sovereign debt, and regulatory rules mean banks can hold fewer bonds. Their participation can help markets function smoothly in an era of increased government borrowing, while their more frequent trading activity boosts liquidity. "Everyone kind of appreciates the role hedge funds play," said Marion Le Morhedec, Fidelity International's chief investment officer, fixed income. But popular hedge fund trades are crowded and are typically funded by debt, while funds' short-term focus means they can suddenly exit en masse if markets move against them, draining liquidity and exacerbating price moves. Hedge funds "completely wipe out the market in those circumstances," Le Morhedec said. "For me, 100% of the explanation (of early October's low liquidity) is this." Asked about the systemic threat posed by hedge funds, the chief financial officer of Wall Street giant JPMorgan told analysts on Tuesday the industry has been "a source of risk for the system for a long time now, and everyone knows that, including the hedge funds themselves". Their leverage is "in the category of known unknowns," Jeremy Barnum said. "It doesn't mean it's riskless, but we kind of know what it is." ON WATCH In early October, short-dated debt was particularly volatile. France's 2-year bond yield surged, Germany's plunged on safe-haven inflows and the gap between the two widened 21 bps, the most in a day since 2012. Hedge funds often use French government bonds as collateral when borrowing to fund their bets. French debt makes up about €100 billion ($112 billion) of the €250 billion in euro zone government bonds that have been pledged for borrowings in the repo market, Bank of France data shows. The Bank of England is also watching the repo market, a crucial source of funding for financial firms at times of stress. It estimates £85 billion ($113 billion) of the £200 billion net borrowing in gilt repo markets is [USN:L6N45R0WM TEXT:"from hedge funds"]. One big European bond investor told Reuters that hedge funds' role has become a key topic for regulators when they meet with the firm. Pictet's Renaud-Chatelain said liquidity in French bonds in early October had been the worst since 2008. Poor liquidity makes trading harder and brokers charge more. In extremis, they may not provide prices at all, causing markets to seize up. A separate IMF report on Tuesday said markets have [USN:L1N45Z031 TEXT:"managed recent stress well"], however, and the half-dozen fund managers Reuters spoke to said that in general the volatility had not yet affected their strategies, and at times created opportunities. "Volatility sometimes is good ... (French debt) became relatively cheap compared to the credit risk," said Michela Bariletti, chief credit officer at Standard Life. "We look at OATs (French bonds) cautiously but during the sell-off, we actually added a bit." ($1 = 0.8929 euros) ($1 = 0.7543 pounds)

item.title: How Healey's first UK budget could ripple through markets
item.description: Britain's new finance minister, John Healey, delivers his first budget on October 28 against a backdrop of rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the Iran war.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Indyk, Medha Singh
item.content:encoded: Britain's new finance minister, [USN:L8N45X047 TEXT:"John Healey"], delivers his first budget on October 28 against a backdrop of rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the Iran war . "This budget is about credibility," said Luke Hickmore, investment director, fixed income, at Aberdeen Investments. Healey "has said fiscal discipline will be at its core, and the gilt market will hold him to that. Stick to the plan and yields might have room to fall. Surprise the market and the bill could arrive quickly." Here is a look at what is at stake for UK markets. BOND SELLOFF STINGS A brutal global bond selloff that pushed the 30-year gilt yield briefly above 6% in October has eroded the [USN:L8N45V18B TEXT:"government's fiscal buffer"], which stood at £24 billion ($31.78 billion) in March. Economists estimate this headroom now stands between roughly £8.5 billion and £16 billion as higher borrowing costs lift the debt interest bill. Healey is under pressure to show how he can meet fiscal rules without raising the main taxes. Bond investors want reassurance over fiscal discipline. Still, sentiment has improved due to relative political stability, [USN:L8N4610AT TEXT:"better economic data"] and the Bank of England's decision to [USN:L8N4590W3 TEXT:"pause its gilt sales"]. "There's a fiscal risk premium in the UK, but maybe it looks less bad than some of the other countries," BofA's head of global G10 FX strategy, Adarsh Sinha, said. STERLING SHRUGS OFF BUDGET RISK Sterling, near 16-month peaks against the euro , does not appear too fazed by the budget. Trading in FX options markets suggests the budget is not shaping up as a key risk event, BofA's Sinha said. "But of course, you never want to get too complacent with the UK budgets because we have the memory of prior budgets, and never say never." Former Prime Minister [USN:L1N460035 TEXT:"Liz Truss' 2022 mini-budget"] triggered a bond and sterling rout by announcing big tax cuts. Nomura's head of G10 FX strategy, Dominic Bunning, said he was watching the degree to which the government looks to use public financial institutions as vehicles to borrow funds, which could test its credibility. "That's something I'm watching with a modest amount of concern about whether that could be more of a negative catalyst for sterling," he said. TAX THE BANKS? As the government looks for additional revenue to shore up its public finances without imposing broad tax rises, [USN:L6N45N0XP TEXT:"banks are sensitive"] to any signs that they could be targeted for a tax raid. Healey is [USN:L8N4610PT TEXT:"poised to tax banks"] in the budget for additional revenue, the Guardian newspaper reported on Thursday. Analysts covering British banks have in recent weeks suggested an increase in the 3% surcharge that banks pay on their profits is likely, with both a return to the previous 8% level and a smaller rise of 2-3 percentage points seen as options. The surcharge currently raises just over £1 billion ($1.3 billion) a year. Shares of the big four banks - HSBC (HSBA.L) , NatWest (NWG.L) , Lloyds (LLOY.L) and Barclays (BARC.L) - are down between 3% and 5% in October so far. While this is broadly in line with other European banks given [USN:L1N45N0S4 TEXT:"higher global borrowing costs"], pre-budget jitters are partly to blame. BUILDERS SET FOR BUDGET BOOST? Housebuilder stocks (.FTNMX402020) surged in late September after the government confirmed plans for a new first-time buyer support scheme in October's budget, boosting a sector battered by weak demand and affordability pressures. "We believe this is the big catalyst the sector as a whole needed for a re-rating," said RBC analyst Anthony Codling after the plans were announced. "Christmas has come early for the UK housebuilders." Still, rising mortgage rates have since acted as a headwind for the sector, with pre-budget share gains being wiped out. UTILITIES ON A WARNING British Prime Minister Andy Burnham put utility companies on warning in a key speech last month, stepping up his rhetoric on [USN:S8N42A057 TEXT:"public ownership"] of underperforming water companies. Burnham also announced [USN:FWN45K0WM TEXT:"Great British Grid"] (GB Grid), a new publicly owned networks company, aimed at cutting energy costs and speeding up connections. "We remain positive on the outlook for UK utilities after various policy announcements," JPMorgan said in a note. "We do not see the announcement of GB Grid ... as a significant threat to the growth and value creation targets of the electricity network companies." Britain's utilities sector (.FTUB6510) is up almost 4% since Burnham's pronouncements; the broader market (.FTLC) is little changed.

item.title: Europe's carmakers set course for managed decline
item.description: Brussels struck a deal to limit Chinese imports and will prop up EU manufacturing. While that’s a relief for €34 bln VW or Stellantis, Beijing’s rivals like BYD are building continental factories and muscling in on premium cars. Europe’s champions will struggle to keep up.
item.dc:creator: Aimee Donnellan
item.content:encoded: At this year’s Paris Motor Show, two competing visions of the future were on display. On Sunday evening, Xpeng (9868.HK) , one of China’s many EV upstarts, hosted clients at an event where Vice Chairman Brian Gu touted humanoid robots, driverless and flying cars. Across town, Volkswagen (VOWG.DE) CEO Oliver Blume, was presenting the German group’s affordable electric vehicles, while calling for more industry support, with giant excerpts of EU treaties pasted on the wall. Relying on Europe, however, may still leave the carmakers on the road to managed decline. Blume's faith in Brussels makes sense. Pressure from Chinese carmakers is forcing the European Commission to take action to protect European champions. Chinese branded cars captured [USN:L6N44S0I1 TEXT:"9%"] of the European market in the first half of the year. AlixPartners, a consultancy, expects Middle Kingdom marques will account for 16% of wider European sales by 2030. BYD (002594.SZ) illustrates the rapid rise of Chinese carmakers in Europe. Its market share in Europe has risen to 2.5% , more than twice what it was the previous year. It now often outsells Tesla (TSLA.O) and Ford Motor (F.N) . The block in [USN:L8N3IQ15T TEXT:"2024"] imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, and is now moving to close the loophole left from those levies by also tackling cars that pair a battery with a combustion engine. Such hybrids accounted for [USN:L6N45Y02E TEXT:"44%"] of China’s auto exports to Europe in the first seven months of this year, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association. Following on quickly from that, it should soon unveil rules that will subsidise cars made on the continent and penalise imports. These measures may offer some relief, but are unlikely to fully contain the Chinese threat. Take hybrids. Brussels last week managed to persuade Beijing to limit exports of these cars to Europe to 350,000 units from December, compared with 302,000 in 2025. The EU expected Chinese imports to reach 800,000 without the cap. Yet the deal only lasts four years, and even during that period BYD and peers can then increase annual sales by 6% a year. They may also be able to sell more cars from hubs outside China, circumventing the limits. The next strand of Brussels' defense are the "Made in Europe" rules. These would mean that cars have to have a minimum proportion of parts made within the bloc to qualify for national subsidies and tax benefits. The idea is that China’s carmakers will either lose share, or be forced to move production into European factories in order to qualify. That may ultimately push up their costs, blunting the current competitive edge that comes from cheap Chinese labour and energy. But there are limits to the deal. To start, “Made in Europe” is not yet law, despite increasingly anxious [USN:B5N443015 TEXT:"calls"] from France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, to curb Chinese imports. Part of the problem is European countries can’t agree on what "Made in Europe" means. Hardliners such as France are pushing a strict interpretation, meaning only factories and suppliers within the EU’s 27 countries count. But Germany has suggested it wants to include states that have close economic ties including the UK. An EU-only approach, which looks increasingly likely, may be better for European jobs, but damage European carmakers’ existing supply chains and push up costs. These disputes may soon be resolved. But the regime will take time to be passed into law, and for subsidies to apply, giving Chinese carmakers time to keep growing market share in electric vehicles without having to rush to set up new factories. This sentiment was clear from Stella Li, BYD’s most senior international executive, who said in Paris the Chinese carmaker is still [USN:L6N45Y0J7 TEXT:"shopping"] around for another location for a European factory and is still not mass producing cars from its [USN:L1N42H0V6 TEXT:"Hungarian plant."] Moreover, Chinese groups are preparing for a pinch by moving up the value chain. In Paris BYD, Xpeng and Li Auto (2015.HK) displayed ever more luxurious, larger cars, which may be less impacted by the Made in Europe rules. Xpeng’s G9L, its flagship SUV with massage chairs, will be sold in Germany for around €75,000, competing head on with BMW’s iX brand. Europeans are fighting back, but also looking to the past. In Paris Citroen, owned by Stellantis (STLAM.MI) , unveiled an electric version of its iconic 2CV. The pitch is budget nostalgia. The car will be sold for a relatively affordable €15,000, including a removable picnic basket, and the design plays on younger buyers’ affection for their childhood family cars. But once again Europeans are targeting the wrong audience. Around 60% of new car sales in Europe are bought by companies and fleet managers who are more likely to want sleek SUVs packed with the latest tech rather than canvas-roofed throwbacks to the 1950s. Nostalgia won’t solve European carmakers bigger problem: their relative lack of efficiency. Chinese groups have fewer brands, and can get them to market more quickly. Whereas groups like Stellantis or Volkswagen are struggling with underused factories and many aged brands. The German group is embarking on a big restructuring that will see it slash [USN:L6N44S0I1 TEXT:"100,000 jobs"], but that may take time. Meanwhile Chinese players will continue to pull ahead in new technologies, such as solid state batteries . Investors are well aware of these potholes. Despite a wave of quirky new models and protection from Brussels, European carmakers are still trading at knockdown prices. VW is worth less than 4 times its expected earnings, per LSEG data, and Stellantis’s valuation has fallen from nearly 7 times to under 5 times in just one year. In Paris, the contrast was stark. European carmakers pointed to their history as proof of their resilience and importance to the continent, while their Chinese rivals looked to the future. Xpeng founder He Xiaopeng talked about how his self-driving car had been cruising around Paris, teaching its software to handle narrower streets and less predictable drivers. Until European carmakers show they are ready for what’s next, the road will continue to narrow. Follow Aimee Donnellan on LinkedIn .

item.title: Asian Cup remains on track but golf tournament postponed in wake of Riyadh attack
item.description: The Asian Cup soccer tournament is on track to take place in Saudi Arabia early next year, local organisers said on Friday, but golf's Asian Tour has postponed the Saudi International indefinitely in the aftermath of a deadly attack on Riyadh.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Asian Cup soccer tournament is on track to take place in Saudi Arabia early next year, local organisers said on Friday, but golf's Asian Tour has postponed the Saudi International indefinitely in the aftermath of a deadly attack on Riyadh. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed responsibility for Saturday's [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"strike on Riyadh's international airport"], which killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. Australia also withdrew its team from the urban cycling World Championships on Friday, citing safety concerns over travelling to Riyadh, where the event is scheduled to take place in early November. The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has already been moved from October to December, while FIFA on Thursday [USN:L1N46108R TEXT:"postponed the FIFAe Finals 2026"] video game competition in the Saudi capital until an unspecified future date. In that environment, serious questions were being asked over whether the 24-team Asian Cup could still go ahead in Saudi Arabia from January 7 to February 5 next year. Asian soccer chief Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said earlier this week that a postponement of the continental championships [USN:L1N4600SG TEXT:"until 2028"] was possible if necessary, but the local organising committee said on Friday they were sticking to the original schedule. "Preparations across all organisational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services," it said in a statement. "(The LOC) will continue to monitor developments relevant to the tournament and ensure the appropriate conditions are in place for its successful delivery." ATTACKS DISRUPT SPORTS CALENDAR The $5 million [USN:L4N4620G5 TEXT:"Saudi International"] , which is sponsored by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), is the flagship event on the Asian Tour and had been scheduled to take place at Riyadh Golf Club from November 18-21. "The decision to postpone was taken following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and ensuring the event is delivered to a standard befitting its international stature," an Asian Tour statement said. AusCycling said its decision to withdraw the Australian team from the urban World Championships was made "with the safety and wellbeing of our athletes and staff our highest priority". The Australian government is advising travellers to "reconsider" trips to Saudi Arabia in general and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport in particular "due to recent security incidents". The Saudi government has invested heavily in sport through the PIF in recent years and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting the soccer World Cup in 2034. According to a report on US news website Semafor earlier this week, PIF is preparing to tell FIFA that it will be scaling back stadium plans for the 2034 tournament as part of a broader review of domestic spending. Reuters has contacted PIF for comment.

item.title: US holds more secret talks with Myanmar's military-backed rulers in Tokyo, sources say
item.description: The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis, Poppy McPherson, John Geddie
item.content:encoded: The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup. Earlier talks in Myanmar's capital Naypyitaw in mid-September focused on securing the release of an American businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously [USN:L6N45T16N TEXT:"reported"]. It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week's talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting. US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar. The State Department did not respond to a request for comment on the latest talks, but says it engages with all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests. A spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment. Asked about its role in hosting the talks, Japan's Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement it had been "communicating as necessary" with both sides but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges. Last month's meeting in Naypyitaw between Vance and Myanmar's coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously told Reuters. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going. A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar's help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said. Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar's leaders are serious about enforcement. Myanmar's military-backed government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres. US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar's large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: the deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role. The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country. "This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country," the State Department said of the sanctions move. Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and crushing a subsequent popular uprising, and the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington [USN:S0N2TK07R TEXT:"declared a genocide"]. The armed forces have killed thousands of people in airstrikes since the putsch, which sparked widespread civil war, the United Nations says. The latest engagements in Japan show the Trump administration views Myanmar through a "purely transactionalist lens," said Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank. "The critical minerals and rare earths that Myanmar holds are viewed as probably the chief strategic asset that Washington is interested in within Myanmar," Marston said. JAPAN'S ROLE UNCLEAR It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar. Japan's acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of Myanmar's military-backed government earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognise the administration. That meeting followed a September visit by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyitaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper. Japan's Foreign Ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe's trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and "does not in any way prejudge" the position of the government. Watanabe told Reuters his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalise relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained. Japan condemned the military's 2021 overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government but stopped short of joining the US and other Western governments in imposing sanctions on junta leaders and military-linked entities. Tokyo was one of Myanmar's largest foreign investors, seeking to counter China's influence in one of Asia's last frontier markets. Unlike numerous Western firms, many Japanese companies remained despite the turmoil that followed the 2021 coup. Around 300 Japanese companies still operate in Myanmar, down from more than 400 in 2020, according to Japan's trade promotion agency, JETRO.

item.title: Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is 'disgrace', Trump says
item.description: Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is a 'disgrace' that keeps global energy prices elevated, US President Donald Trump told the Newsmax news outlet in an interview aired on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Jekaterina Golubkova
item.content:encoded: Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is a 'disgrace' that keeps global energy prices elevated, US President Donald Trump told the Newsmax news outlet in an interview aired on Thursday. Ukraine [USN:L6N4610BB TEXT:"struck"] a Russian oil refinery after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites that Trump had announced, and criticised his willingness to strike deals with Moscow. "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said in the interview, after Ukraine hit a Rosneft (ROSN.MM) refinery southeast of Moscow which helps to supply the Russian capital. "There are a lot of targets you can hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he's not doing a good service for the world." Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, targeting energy facilities such as power stations, knocking out supply to hundreds of thousands, and Zelenskiy told the Financial Times that Ukraine's patience had run out. Trump's administration has been trying to mediate a ceasefire deal to end the war that started with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He repeated to Newsmax his belief that Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin hate each other, which makes it hard to end the conflict. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskiy," Trump said. "I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelenskiy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin." As Trump pressured Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukraine [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"faced"] reduced usage of a satellite system on which it relies for battlefield communications and drone operations. The order came from inside the White House, [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"said"] two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter, without specifying who there made the decision or was responsible for implementing the order.

item.title: Fed's Warsh sees US resilience, mum on rate-path view
item.description: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh voiced optimism on Friday about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been "hanging in there" amid continued energy shocks and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation.
item.dc:creator: David Lawder, Leika Kihara
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh voiced optimism on Friday about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been "hanging in there" amid continued energy shocks and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation. He said the US and many other economies were benefiting from an "investment surge" driven by artificial intelligence but broadening to other sectors that was creating a near-term demand shock that was putting upward pressure on inflation. "I came out of meetings here yesterday and today and it's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," Warsh said at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. With inflation a "common challenge," Warsh said global central banks undertook "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world, and that means there's no free riders." In the US, he said, "We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," in a reference to the Fed's September interest-rate hike. NO PREVIEW OF RATE PATH But in keeping with his style since taking the reins as Fed chief in May, he gave no preview about whether he feels more interest-rate hikes will be needed, or when. "I don't prejudge meetings," Warsh added in the discussion with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. "I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year." Warsh's colleagues at the Fed have not been reticent on their rate-path views. In recent weeks nearly all said they feel more tightening is probably needed, but most wanted to see more economic data in order to assess the inflation trend, a signal that they were unlikely to deliver a second rate hike this month. Financial markets have taken those remarks on board and are betting the Fed will wait until December to raise rates. That remained true even after reports this week showed two [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"different measures"] of inflation [USN:L1N4610KT TEXT:"running higher"] than expected and heading in the wrong direction from the Fed's 2% goal. Warsh's decision to skirt the near-term policy decision altogether and stick to broader economic themes leaves intact the expectation that the Fed will not hike this month. 'BUMPY' AI PATH TO MORE WEALTH Warsh was optimistic about the impact of AI on economic growth and productivity in the medium-term, even as he said it would be a "very bumpy" path toward what he expected would be faster productivity growth in the "real economy" that would bolster wealth. "It's obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it's going to hit the supply side of the economy," he said. "We don't know in the next 12 or 18 months its effect on employment, but if you believe like I believe, which is it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive, that it's going to make it so that we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very good thing." A task force convened to advise the Fed on the impact of AI on productivity and jobs will hold a "field hearing" in the San Francisco Bay Area on November 16, he said, in what will be a first public peek at the group's work. EMERGING STRONGER He said a broadening of the investment surge beyond AI was providing some resilience to US growth. "It means we've got plenty of tailwinds that are giving some strength and durability to this economy," he said. "That sort of momentum is certainly not found everywhere in the world." But the global economy, too, was "showing resilience that I'm not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago, given what's happening in geopolitics and hotspots around the world." The IMF earlier this week said that AI investment would [USN:L1N45Z01U TEXT:"keep global growth above 3%"] this year, partly offsetting the drag from oil prices that are hovering above $100 per barrel, but risks from high debt loads and a potential sharp pullback in AI investment and asset values threaten the outlook. Warsh said that central bankers meeting in Bangkok had a common vision to safeguard price stability and were taking action to back that view, which was giving "confidence to businesses and households that's so important for growth to continue." "I believe optimistically — you might think naively — at least in the United States, we're going to come out of this stronger with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth," Warsh said.

item.title: India's Yes Bank expects AT1 reinstatement to cut core capital ratio by 250 bps
item.description: India's Yes Bank said on Friday it expects the reinstatement of its previously written-off additional tier-1 (AT1) bonds to reduce its core capital ratio by about 250 basis points.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India's Yes Bank (YESB.NS) said on Friday it expects the reinstatement of its previously written-off additional tier-1 (AT1) bonds to reduce its core capital ratio by about 250 basis points. On Thursday, the country's top court [USN:L4N4610SV TEXT:"set aside"] the bank's write-off of 84 billion rupees ($883.7 million) in additional tier-1 bonds during its 2020 rescue, dealing a blow to the lender and regulators that had defended the move. Here are some details: Capital ratios measure a bank's financial strength by comparing its capital with its risk-weighted assets, indicating its ability to withstand losses Yes Bank's tier-1 capital ratio would remain unchanged at 14% on a pro forma basis, the bank said Yes Bank said it is reviewing the ruling and its implications and will make further disclosures "in due course" Separately, S&P Global Ratings said it does not expect India’s Supreme Court ruling against Yes Bank to affect its ratings, though it would weigh on future earnings Yes Bank’s regulatory capital is adequate, with its common equity tier-1 ratio of 13.87% as of end-March 2026 able to absorb the expected 250 bps hit while staying well above the 5.5% minimum requirement, S&P said S&P expects the roughly 84 billion-rupee hit to common equity to be largely offset by the reinstatement of the bonds It said that the lender's credit profile can withstand the ruling, which addresses procedural lapses in the write-down under the 2020 rescue The ratings agency expects Yes Bank to remain adequately capitalized, with its risk-adjusted capital ratio projected to remain between 8% and 8.5% through March 2028, compared with 9% in March 2026 It was unclear whether Yes Bank would challenge the ruling, S&P said ($1 = 95.0550 Indian rupees)

item.title: Modi's predicament: Gen Z pours out on India's streets as dissent surges
item.description: Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, with people under 30 making up nearly one quarter of the country's 1 billion voters.
item.dc:creator: Tora Agarwala, Saurabh Sharma, Sunil Kataria
item.content:encoded: Despite tens of thousands of security personnel deployed to stop them, youth protesters in India scaled barricades last week, chanted anti-government slogans and scuffled with police officers trying to drag them away. "Long live the revolution," shouted one young man before police bundled him into a bus. Street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade, the independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) Project has said, as dissent mounts against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government and Gen Z activists pour on to the streets. Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, with people under 30 making up nearly one quarter of the country's 1 billion voters. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029. "The nation has suddenly found its voice," said Yogendra Yadav, an anti-government activist who has played a leading part in the demonstrations. "I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral". The government and Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party declined comment for this story. The recent protests in the capital Delhi and elsewhere were focused on demands that Election Commission chief [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] resign over a [USN:L4N45K0E7 TEXT:"voter roll revision"] that activists and opposition parties say favours the BJP and has helped it win several recent state elections. The ruling BJP, the government and the Election Commission deny the accusations. The BJP says the party's wins have come from Modi's popularity and strong economic growth. But the demonstrations are also reflecting something larger: growing anger at Modi for failing to deliver jobs to millions of unemployed youth in his 12 years in power despite the surge in headline economic growth. Other issues have also fed into the anti-establishment mood, including leaks of question papers in [USN:L4N43O0C9 TEXT:"key examinations"] for jobs and education, the high number of crimes against women and the rise of billionaire businessmen alleged to have close links to Modi. Modi has a strongman image and his government has previously cracked down on pockets of dissent harshly, but that hasn't fazed the youngsters on the streets. "The fear in us is gone," said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who was part of massive protests in the capital on Saturday. Speaking after she clung to the windscreen wipers of a bus that police were using to detain protesters, Raturi said: "We don't fear being detained or beaten up by the police. This generation enjoys it." Police have denied allegations that they beat up people at the demonstrations, saying protesters were handled according to prescribed procedures. REUTERS/Priyanshu Singh THE RISE OF THE COCKROACHES The protests have been energised by the emergence of the first nationally resonant youth-led movement of the Modi era, the [USN:L4N45W00W TEXT:"Cockroach Janta Party"], which grew from online satire into a nationwide campaign this June after India's chief justice likened the unemployed to "cockroaches". India's mainstream media is mostly pro-government, critics say, and has covered the protests sparingly. But thousands of protesters armed with mobile phones as well as independent news channels on YouTube have amplified the unrest and made Internet stars of leaders like CJP founder [USN:L1N45W01X TEXT:"Abhijeet Dipke"] and firebrand left-wing activist [USN:L4N45X011 TEXT:"Neha Bora"]. Opposition parties that were subdued under Modi's grip on power have been re-energised, with Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi and tens of thousands of followers also on the streets. The unrest has drawn comparisons with neighbouring Bangladesh and Nepal, where youth-led protest movements brought down governments in recent years, although analysts caution that India's political landscape and Modi's popularity make such parallels imperfect. Many of the youth protesters grew up during Modi's rise to power, buoyed by promises of jobs, opportunity and cleaner governance. A decade later, many say those aspirations remain unfulfilled and they say the Hindu nationalist government appears more focused on religious issues and divisive politics against minorities, especially Muslims. Ananya Raturi, 21, reacts as she tries to stop the police bus carrying detained protesters during a protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, October 10, 2026. REUTERS/Priyanshu Singh/File Photo The government has previously said the economy generated 168.3 million new jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of any bias, saying his government works for all Indians. 30-year-old Gauri Seth, a medical student based in Kolkata, became a voter in 2014, the same year the Modi government came to power. Seth said the Modi government promised "a lot, but has failed to deliver." "Instead they focus on things like religious infrastructure. There are cases of violence against minorities. When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition." IT'S MOSTLY ABOUT JOBS When Modi came to power, he promised the creation of millions of jobs each year. Yet, despite India's strong economic growth since then, unemployment remains at slightly above 5%, according to government data. A Reuters poll last year said that data masks the [USN:L4N3TC0XX TEXT:"severity of joblessness"], especially among the youth. Unemployment among the 367 million people in the country aged 15-29 stood at 9.9% in 2025, according to the data. Research by Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 report found unemployment among graduates aged 15-25 was nearly 40%, while about one in five graduates aged 25-29 remained jobless. In May, unrest erupted across the country when the government invalidated examinations for national medical colleges, a pathway to jobs for the poor and the middle class , after test papers were leaked. Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in Delhi, said repeated examination paper leaks had deepened a sense among young Indians that the system was denying them opportunities even after years of study. "This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities," she said. Neha Bora, National President of the All India Students' Association (AISA), reacts as she is detained by police during a protest against alleged assault on female protestors and journalists by Delhi Police and demanding resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, October 4, 2026. REUTERS/Bhawika Chhabra/File Photo While national elections are not due for almost three years, the country's biggest state, Uttar Pradesh, goes to the polls early next year, which could provide a test of Modi's popularity. Analysts however remain cautious about the outcome. The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago, said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi. "But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say."

item.title: Power, bullpen steer Brewers to NLCS sweep, first Series bid since '82
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Their rallying cry was "Our way," and in the end, the Milwaukee Brewers plowed their way into the franchise's first World Series appearance in 44 years by doing it every way possible.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: LOS ANGELES -- Their rallying cry was "Our way," and in the end, the Milwaukee Brewers plowed their way into the franchise's first World Series appearance in 44 years by doing it every way possible. Clutch hitting, pitching and even a newly discovered power game lifted the Brewers to a four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series. Jake Bauers started the Brewers' Game 4 comeback with a two-run double and Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead home run to deliver a 6-4 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday. Bauers added a bases-loaded walk to tie the game in the fifth inning as the Brewers rallied from an early four-run to become the first team to sweep the same club that swept them out of the playoffs one year prior. "They have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we have a bunch of gamers, and the gamers won this week," Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said at the on-field trophy presentation. Catcher William Contreras guided the Brewers' pitching staff in a bullpen game, and four pitchers held the Dodgers scoreless over the final seven innings. JoJo Romero (2-1) tossed two innings, and Aaron Ashby handled the final three frames for his second save of the postseason. Bauers was selected the Most Valuable Player of the NLCS after going 4-for-14 (.286) with one homer and six RBIs. "I can't speak for anybody else, but for me, watching the way they carried themselves on the field after sweeping us last year was a little bit eye-opening," Bauers said. "Those guys swept us, they sent us home, and you would have thought it was a handshake line at a spring training game. That's something that I carried with me. That's something that I remembered. "Yeah, it was a little bit of motivation to just say, 'We've got to keep going until there's not another game left to play.'" The Brewers will open the World Series at home on Oct. 23 against the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays. The Guardians hold a 2-1 lead after winning 3-2 on Thursday. Milwaukee made its only previous World Series appearance as an AL team in 1982, falling in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals. Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani hit a three-run homer in his return to the leadoff spot but also struck out three times while playing with knee and biceps discomfort that will be addressed in the offseason. "I was grateful to spend time together as a team," Ohtani said through an interpreter. "Although we fell short, and are definitely disappointed, I want to use this as a catalyst to have a better season as a team (next year)." Dodgers starter Tyler Glasnow gave up four runs on three hits and two walks over 4 1/3 innings. He struck out six. Tanner Scott (0-1) served up Mitchell's go-ahead home run in the sixth inning. Los Angeles was trying to become the first National League club to win three consecutive World Series titles. "I can't give enough praise to the Brewers organization," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "... I think for me it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better. I had a good conversation with the guys in (the Los Angeles locker room) and just told them how proud I was. "I'm not used to consolation speeches, but it was a long season. It was still a good season." The Dodgers appeared to be all business in the second inning when Andy Pages delivered a one-out RBI single and Ohtani added a towering three-run blast with two outs for a 4-0 advantage. Bauers continued his impressive series in the fourth inning with a two-run ground-rule double to cut Milwaukee's deficit in half. David Hamilton pulled the Brewers within 4-3 in the fifth inning with an RBI single, ending Glasnow's outing. Dodgers reliever Evan Phillips subsequently loaded the bases with two outs on a pair of walks. Alex Vesia replaced Phillips and walked Bauers on four pitches to tie the game. Milwaukee went up for good in the sixth at 5-4 when Mitchell, a Southern California native and UCLA alumnus, greeted Scott with a leadoff home run. The Dodgers wasted a one-out double from Kyle Tucker in the sixth inning and a leadoff double from Pages in the seventh. Another double combined with an error in the eighth put Will Smith on third base as the potential tying run with one out. Ashby then retired Tucker on a shallow fly ball and struck out Teoscar Hernandez to end the threat. Hamilton sealed the victory with a two-out home run in the ninth inning against Edwin Diaz. "You guys talk to me all the time and hear my nonsense, but the truth is these guys are a special group," Murphy said of his players. "They're together. They care about each other. I love the Dodgers. I love their players. They've got legendary players. But we came in with a group that would not be denied." --Doug Padilla, Field Level Media

item.title: Winger Nawaqanitawase to make decision on international future next year
item.description: Dual-code winger Mark Nawaqanitawase said on Friday he will decide on his international future next year and that he is only focused on his next move to Japanese club Wild Knights.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Dual-code winger Mark Nawaqanitawase said on Friday he will decide on his international future next year and that he is only focused on his next move to Japanese club Wild Knights. Wallabies coach Les Kiss is keen to secure Nawaqanitawase for the Rugby World Cup but the player's agent [USN:L4N45Z0F5 TEXT:"said"] this week there was no guarantee he would play for the national team again given he would also qualify for Fiji or Italy midway through next year. Nawaqanitawase responded to the speculation in a post on social media. “My only focus right now is moving to Japan in a couple of weeks and connecting with my new team at Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights," said the 26-year-old, who has Fijian and Italian heritage through his parents. “I will weigh up my options and make a decision next year on my international future." Nawaqanitawase finished up his spell with the Sydney Roosters after his tries helped them to the National Rugby League (NRL) [USN:L4N45Q016 TEXT:"title"] earlier this month and is returning to the 15-man game on a two-year deal with the Wild Knights. Kiss confirmed the winger would not join the Wallabies for November's Nations Championship tests in Europe but thought he would be back in the green and gold of Australia before next year's World Cup on home soil. "We've had a couple of chats and (we were) always waiting for the end of the year to see where he sits," Kiss told reporters. "He's had a big year, a fantastic year, hasn't he? So the conversations are being wrapped around making sure we get what's right for him. "I think there's no doubt that you know he wants to be back in the game for us, that's for sure." Kiss, himself a former rugby league winger, said Nawaqanitawase would need some time to readjust to rugby union and was not certain to come straight back into the side. "Everyone will earn their way," he said. "But if he's playing good footy, he'll be in the mix, that's for sure. "It's a different game in terms of height and how you attack the game, how you move in the game, how you defend, how the aerial game is different, so he's got a lot of things just to relearn. "Won't take him long, that's for sure." Nawaqanitawase made 11 appearances for the Wallabies before switching to the NRL, where he built a reputation as one of the game's biggest aerial threats as well as someone able to conjure up stunning tries.

item.title: Philippines hits back at Chinese envoy over 'thinly veiled threat' of force
item.description: The Philippines has chided China's ambassador for what it interpreted as a "thinly veiled threat" of force, after Beijing's envoy said his country would prevail in a confrontation between them.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Philippines has chided China's ambassador for what it interpreted as a "thinly veiled threat" of force, after Beijing's envoy said his country would prevail in a confrontation between them. Here are some details: The Philippine foreign ministry said Ambassador Jing Quan's remarks to journalists on Thursday were a "poor choice of words" and unhelpful given their complicated bilateral ties Jing had said China "may easily win" but would not use force as "we love peace" The ambassador was asked for his reaction to the Philippine defence secretary calling China a regional "troublemaker" Their comments were the latest heated exchange between China and US defence ally the Philippines, which have repeatedly sparred over disputed features in the South China Sea Asked on Friday about the ambassador's remarks, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said it "sounds very much like a threat" deserving of a discussion with the envoy The Chinese embassy said the ambassador had been selectively quoted and called Manila's response an "over-interpretation", adding relations were currently "at an extremely sensitive stage" China's foreign ministry said Beijing's position on improving and developing relations with Manila is clear and it hopes that the Philippine side will understand it "accurately and comprehensively” The Philippines and China have been at loggerheads for years over reefs and islands in the South China Sea located in the Philippine exclusive economic zone, with their coast guards squaring off repeatedly

item.title: Indonesia's president ready to accept foreign assistance to combat fires, foreign minister says
item.description: Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto has agreed to accept assistance from neighbouring countries to tackle its worst forest fires in more than a decade, the country's foreign minister said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto has agreed to accept assistance from neighbouring countries to tackle its worst forest fires in more than a decade, the country's foreign minister said. Indonesia has come under heavy criticism after months of [USN:L6N4610Y7 TEXT:"fierce wildfires"] that have caused respiratory problems for hundreds of thousands of people and spread thick haze into neighbouring countries, leading to school closures in [USN:L6N4600NO TEXT:"Malaysia and East Timor"]. Last month, Malaysia offered to deploy three helicopters, an aircraft, and 52 personnel to help contain the fires, but there has been no follow-up since. Singapore, another country badly affected by the haze, has also said it is ready to step in to help contain the fires. "The President has already expressed his approval, and the matter is currently being discussed at the technical level within the BNPB," Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said, according to a voice a recording shared by his ministry on Friday. BNPB is Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency. The new chief of the agency, appointed on Thursday, said he is [USN:L6N4610HK TEXT:"reviewing"] the types of assistance being offered and will decide which ones can be accelerated. The islands of Sumatra and Borneo, close to Singapore and Malaysia, have been the worst affected, with the fire able smoulder slowly beneath the surface of large stretches of peatland and re-emerge at any moment. Fire also spread to the national park of Mount Bromo in East Java, where four people involved in fighting fires were killed, the Forestry Ministry said in a statement on Friday. Two others are undergoing medical treatment for severe burns.

item.title: Indonesian stocks sink most since 1998 on MSCI downgrade warning
item.description: Indonesian stocks suffered their steepest one-day fall in 28 years on Friday after MSCI said the country was no longer worthy of emerging market status, threatening billions of dollars in capital outflows from Southeast Asia's largest economy.
item.dc:creator: Sameer Manekar
item.content:encoded:
Indonesian stocks suffered their steepest one-day fall in 28 years on Friday after MSCI said the country was [USN:L4N46124S TEXT:"no longer worthy of "emerging market" status"], threatening billions of dollars in capital outflows from Southeast Asia's largest economy. In a surprise move on Friday, MSCI said it would put Indonesia on a path to a "standalone market" status, worse than the previously flagged "frontier" category. A downgrade would exclude Indonesian stocks from indexes tracked by global funds, potentially triggering billions of dollars in capital outflows. The Jakarta Composite Index (.JKSE) plunged as much as 11.4% to its lowest point since early November 2020, clocking its worst one-day drop since January 1998. Indonesian shares have lost nearly 40% this year, making them the world's worst-performing equity market. "Indonesia's immediate priority should be to demonstrate measurable improvements in market transparency and regulatory enforcement, rather than merely announcing additional reforms," Josua Pardede, chief economist at Bank Permata, said. Foreign investors have pulled $4.6 billion from Indonesian equities this year, as per LSEG data. UBS estimates that removal from global indexes could trigger a further $4 billion in passive outflows and about $15 billion from active investors. If downgraded, Indonesia would join Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, and Ukraine in the standalone category, becoming the only Asia-Pacific market in the group and its largest economy, with a GDP more than twice Argentina's. On Friday, blue-chip stocks, including major lenders, miners, and energy firms, declined nearly 15%, the exchange's lower limit. The rupiah, one of the worst-performing currencies this year, weakened to 18,070 per US dollar, its lowest since late July, before paring losses to 18,000 a dollar. "Conviction has weakened and a pick-up of active fund outflows in the short-term cannot be ruled out," Citi analysts wrote, adding that their base case remains for Indonesia to retain its emerging-market classification. "Continued outflows by active funds have become likelier in our view in light of the latest MSCI downgrade warning. This would come ahead of potentially mid-single-digit billion dollars of passive fund outflows if the downgrade materializes." In East Asia, South Korean stocks (.KS11) rebounded from a 6-month closing low, but remained on track for their biggest weekly loss in 18 years following a brutal selloff on AI worries. Stocks in Taiwan (.TWII) edged higher after an over 3% decline the previous day, while its dollar weakened to late-July lows of 32.520 per US dollar, mainly pressured by equity outflows. An MSCI gauge of emerging Asia equities (.MIMS00000PUS) , dominated by chip stocks in East Asia, rose 1%, but was headed for its worst week since the start of the Middle East war. Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, Singapore stocks (.STI) added 0.5%, while those in the Philippines (.PSI) advanced more than 2%. The Philippine peso recovered from a record low hit on Thursday, last selling at 62.991 a dollar. Stocks in Malaysia (.KLSE) slipped 0.7%. Thai stock markets were closed for a holiday. item.title: Luke Hughes nets 2 goals in Devils' 7-1 domination of Rangers
item.description: Luke Hughes led the way with two of the New Jersey Devils' four second-period goals to help bury their rival New York Rangers 7-1 in Newark, N.J. on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Luke Hughes led the way with two of the New Jersey Devils' four second-period goals to help bury their rival New York Rangers 7-1 in Newark, N.J. on Thursday. Nico Daws stopped 18 shots in the victory, while Nico Hischier, Arseny Gritsyuk, Evan Rodrigues, Cody Glass, and Stefan Noesen all joined Hughes on the scoresheet. Timo Meier, Dougie Hamilton, Brett Pesce, Dawson Mercer, and Amadeus Lombardi all picked up a pair of assists each. Pavel Dorofeyev scored the Rangers' lone goal as they allowed more than three goals for the first time this season. Rodrigues took advantage of a tough giveaway and ripped it past Dylan Garand with 30 seconds remaining in the first period to give the Devils the lead. Hughes fired a point shot that bounced off a defender and snuck through the legs of Garand to double the Devils' advantage just 18 seconds into the middle frame. Hischier then made it 3-0 barely over four minutes into the second. After the Devils captain fired his shot wide on an odd-man rush, he stuck around and poked a rebound past the pad of an outstretched Garand. The Devils kept rolling just 31 seconds later as Gritsyuk made up for a missed breakaway by pouncing on a rebound and lighting the lamp, marking the end of Garand's night after he allowed four goals on 13 shots. Spencer Martin gave up three goals on 18 shots in relief. The youngest Hughes brother showcased his impressive skillset as he walked the blueline and cut in toward the net. He sent a shot off the far post and into the back of the net for his second goal of the night with 3:26 left in the second. Noesen buried his first goal of the season to make it 6-0 with just over seven minutes gone in the third period. Dorofeyev spoiled Daws' shutout bid with a power-play marker just over a minute later. Glass got in on the action to make it 7-1 with just over five minutes left in the contest. --Field Level Media
