item.content:encoded: The US dollar was set for its first weekly fall in more than a month against the euro and the yen, as investors turned their focus to the US rate outlook while concerns about an escalation of the Iran conflict faded. AI stocks have [USN:L6N460140 TEXT:"cratered"] this week and the [USN:L4N46112V TEXT:"stress has spread"] to parts of the credit market as investors who have crowded into bets all along the AI supply chain [USN:L4N46112V TEXT:"worry"] data centre operators might not manage to be profitable in time to pay their debts. Analysts noted that Wednesday's market moves may provide a preview of how currencies would react to a major AI-driven selloff, with the dollar falling instead of attracting safe-haven demand as investors shift towards a more dovish view of the Federal Reserve policy path. The Swiss franc again looks set to be the biggest beneficiary, thanks to its safe-haven status and expectations that, even in a lower-rates environment, Switzerland is unlikely to cut policy rates below the current zero level. It was set for a 0.61% weekly rise versus the dollar. The dollar index , which measures the US currency against six major peers, fell 0.25% to 101.77 and was set for a 0.45% weekly decline. It rose in two of the week's five sessions, including on Wednesday, as the boost from hotter-than-expected inflation data more than offset the drag from a selloff in tech stocks. The S&P 500 [USN:L6N4611C9 TEXT:"ended higher on Thursday"], springing back from early losses as investors concerned about AI stocks shifted into healthcare and consumer stocks. Wednesday’s “action revealed exactly what could threaten the US dollar and bring US yields lower in the next few months and in 2027: a reduction in the outlook for AI investment,” Thierry Wizman, global forex and rates strategist at Macquarie Group, said. “That's because it would reduce bond supply and impair US growth, all else equal,” he added. US RATES IN FOCUS US Treasury yields dropped earlier this week despite [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"hot inflation readings"] as [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"cautious remarks from Federal Reserve officials"] tempered October hike expectations. Markets assign an 87% probability to the Federal Reserve keeping rates unchanged later this month, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. Investors expect US President Donald Trump to steer clear of any escalation in the Middle East or Ukraine, as a broader conflict could hurt his standing ahead of the midterm elections fuelling inflation and possibly hurting the economy. The euro was up 0.14% to $1.1235 after climbing 0.56% on Thursday in its biggest daily rise in two months. It was on track for a 0.39% weekly gain. "Barring another big leg down in AI stocks and risk assets in general, expect the dollar to consolidate near recent highs," said Chris Turner, forex strategist at ING. "It is only when short-end rates break lower that the dollar is ready to drop. And we are not there yet," he added. The yen was on track for a 0.28% weekly rise after dropping for four consecutive weeks as the Iran conflict supported the greenback. It was last up 0.05% at 157.89. Higher oil prices tend to support the dollar while weighing on energy-importing currencies such as the euro and yen. [USN:L6N45A080 TEXT:"The Japanese currency tumbled"] in mid-September after a disappointing Bank of Japan policy meeting, but subsequently fell by around 0.30% a week as monetary tightening rhetoric by Japan's authorities supported the yen. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Friday that the [USN:P8N44Z00F TEXT:"BoJ would continue to raise policy rates"] in line with economic and financial developments. The Australian dollar rose 0.55% to $0.6959 but was an outlier in heading for a fall of 0.3% on the dollar this week, after a surprisingly soft jobs report on Thursday had markets paring back expectations for another rise in interest rates.

item.title: Oil eases but heads for weekly gain as investors focus on Middle East supply
item.description: Oil prices eased on Friday but were heading for weekly gains on uncertainty over Middle East supplies and a larger-than-expected draw from US crude stockpiles, while European diesel margins dropped following the IEA's decision to release more diesel.
item.dc:creator: Enes Tunagur
item.content:encoded: Oil prices eased on Friday but were heading for weekly gains on uncertainty over Middle East supplies and a larger-than-expected draw from US crude stockpiles, while European diesel margins dropped following the IEA's decision to release more diesel. Brent crude futures were down 47 cents, or 0.44%, at $105.45 a barrel by 0747 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 62 cents, or 0.63%, to $97.35. WTI settled up more than 3% on Thursday after a big [USN:L6N46115T TEXT:"US crude stock draw"] on hurricane production shut-ins. For this week so far, Brent has increased 0.72%, while WTI has jumped 5.9%. "Uncertainty in the Middle East and concerns over the sustainability of oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz has the market pricing in a significant risk premium," ING analysts wrote in a note. Some kind of agreement between the US and Iran was required to provide more confidence to the market that stronger oil flows from the region would continue, they added. IRAN SAYS IT IS STEPPING UP STRIKES NEAR STRAIT OF HORMUZ Supply jitters also increased as attacks around [USN:L1N4600JW TEXT:"the Strait of Hormuz"] surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. Total Hormuz clearance averaged 11.62 million barrels per day over the seven days to October 13, about 68% of the 17.15 million bpd baseline, said ship tracking firm Kpler. European diesel refining margins declined by nearly 2% on Friday to $78.67 a barrel, after the International Energy Agency [USN:L1N4610MY TEXT:"agreed"] on Thursday to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market. Those margins rose as high as $95 a barrel in September as diesel supply tightened because of wars in Ukraine and Iran. "Intensified Iranian attacks drove Gulf crude flows sharply lower," Kpler analysts said in a report on Thursday, adding that they expected a slower and more uneven Hormuz recovery in the absence of a comprehensive political deal. The Houthis [USN:L1N4600JW TEXT:"fired"] missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing two guards, while the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen detailed dozens of attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the escalating conflict. The Trump administration is considering [USN:L1N461108 TEXT:"lifting"] sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that have carried oil and petroleum products from countries such as Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in a bid to cut record global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday. The discussions come days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans.

item.title: China says Israel should stop its 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
item.description: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israeli President Isaac Herzog that Israel should stop and reverse its "forced establishment" of West Bank settlements.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israeli President Isaac Herzog that Israel should stop and reverse its "forced establishment" of West Bank settlements. China has consistently held that the Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century, Wang told Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan, according to a statement by the Chinese foreign ministry on Friday. Herzog said in a post on X that the meeting, which took place on Thursday, focused on "relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East". His office declined to comment when asked about their discussions on the West Bank or the Palestinians. Wang said that promoting peace and reconciliation in the region is the "cornerstone" of China's Middle East policy China believes that the "two-state solution" is the right path to a resolution and the immediate priority is to fully open access to the Gaza Strip so a humanitarian "catastrophe" is not allowed to spread, Wang added China is willing to work with the international community to push all parties to return to dialogue and consultation as soon as possible and seek a political settlement of the conflict, Wang said China has long been a supporter of the Palestinian cause and also has close ties with Israel's main regional foe, Iran

item.title: Rotting meat smell sparks protest at Mexico's screwworm sterile-fly plant
item.description: A rotten smell hanging over a town in Mexico's southern Chiapas state drove residents into the streets on Thursday to demand the removal of a sterile-fly plant at the center of the US-Mexican fight against the flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite.
item.dc:creator: Jose Torres, Cassandra Garrison
item.content:encoded: A rotten smell hanging over a town in Mexico's southern Chiapas state drove residents into the streets on Thursday to demand the removal of a sterile-fly plant at the center of the US-Mexican fight against the flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite. Residents in Metapa de Dominguez compared the odor to rotting meat and spoiled food, describing it as “pungent in your nose and mouth” and causing nausea. The smell, once concentrated around the plant, could now be detected farther away, particularly when winds carried it across the town, protesters said. The odor had reached schools near the plant and disrupted classes. "We don't care about the investment they made. What we want is for this plant to leave here, because the smell coming over the town is too much," said truck driver Mercedes Becerra de la Cruz. The complaints come less than four months after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins [USN:L6N42X14F TEXT:"inaugurated"] the facility on June 27. The US Department of Agriculture invested $21 million toward the $51 million facility, part of a broader effort to halt a screwworm outbreak that disrupted the cross-border cattle trade. Sterile flies are the main defense against screwworm, a parasite whose larvae burrow into the living flesh of cattle and other warm-blooded animals and can kill them if untreated. Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports. The Metapa plant is expected eventually to produce 100 million sterile flies a week. Mexico has recorded nearly 48,000 cases of screwworm in the current outbreak and the United States 53. Inside the Metapa plant, millions of flies are bred each week, their larvae fed a carefully formulated mixture of egg, milk and powdered hemoglobin that mimics the nutrient-rich conditions of a wound. The flies are sterilized before being released by the millions to mate with wild females without producing offspring, gradually suppressing the population. Outside its walls, residents said daily life has increasingly been shaped by an overpowering odor that drifts into surrounding neighborhoods and schools. "We need the federal government to respond and have the plant relocated. It is far too close, right in the middle of the town," said 49-year-old homemaker Rosalba Merida Herrera. "For the sake of our children and our elderly, we are asking them to look at the situation, as this issue is now affecting the entire town." A spokesperson for Mexico's Agriculture Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Indonesia gets a 'wake-up call' as MSCI prepares to expel it from global indexes
item.description: Indonesia's stock market is no longer worthy of "emerging market" status, MSCI said on Friday, laying out a plan to remove it from a suite of indexes tracked by funds, a shock move that sparked the steepest one-day drop in Jakarta shares since 1998.
item.dc:creator: Stefanno Sulaiman, Ankur Banerjee
item.content:encoded: Indonesia's stock market is no longer worthy of "emerging market" status, MSCI said on Friday, laying out a plan to remove it from a suite of indexes tracked by funds, a shock move that sparked the steepest one-day drop in Jakarta shares since 1998. The benchmark stock index (.JKSE) , already the world's [USN:L4N43G12X TEXT:"worst performer"] this year, plunged 11% to a six-year low, while the rupiah slid 0.6% to 18,070 per US dollar, its weakest level since late July. Indonesian equities have struggled since January when MSCI froze Indonesia in its indexes and [USN:L6N46202Y TEXT:"threatened a downgrade"] to "frontier" status because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour. On Friday, MSCI said reforms to address those problems have not made sufficient progress and that even a downgrade to frontier wouldn't reflect the severity of issues. "Significant concerns remain around market dysfunction," MSCI said. "Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia's continued classification as an emerging market no longer appropriate," it said in a statement. Instead, it proposed a downgrade to "standalone" status, which would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by billions of dollars in passive investment, forcing funds that follow or are ranked against the indexes to sell. UBS estimated such a move could trigger about $4 billion of passive outflows from Indonesia, with active investors potentially adding a further $15 billion in outflow. Already, foreign investors have net sold $4.7 billion worth of Indonesian stocks in 2026. Coming a month ahead of a scheduled review, MSCI's change of tack [USN:L1N46203P TEXT:"stunned investors"] and irked Jakarta officials. Indonesia's senior economic minister Airlangga Hartarto said there was "a big question mark" over why MSCI did not discuss downgrading the country to "standalone" status during a meeting this week in Bangkok. He made the comment ahead of a meeting of the country's top officials, including the finance minister, the governor of the central bank and other related officials to discuss MSCI's announcement. The Indonesia Stock Exchange said it has taken concrete steps to enhance transparency and integrity in the country's capital market, and CEO Jeffrey Hendrik said he would request further clarification on the basis for the announcement. Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, said the move did not reflect the health of the vast majority of listed companies or indeed the Indonesian economy, and "grouping Indonesia with Lebanon, Palestine, and Argentina does not make sense." "This is a wake-up call for Indonesia," he said. MSCI SCRUTINY RAISES MORE QUESTIONS MSCI's announcement piles pressure on the government under President Prabowo Subianto. Indonesia has faced a series of setbacks this year, with [USN:L4N3Z114D TEXT:"Moody's"] and [USN:L1N3ZS06T TEXT:"Fitch"] cutting their sovereign rating outlooks to negative, citing reduced policymaking credibility. "The proposal highlights MSCI's dissatisfaction with the pace of reforms and raises further questions about the investability of the market," said Tan Altundag, investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management. "The investment implications could be significant," said Altundag, who has no holdings in Indonesia. The office of finance minister Suahasil Nazara, who chairs the country's financial stability board, did not reply to a request for comment. In a sign of investor anxiety over the index provider's move, there was a rush for the exits when the market opened, triggering a 30-minute trading halt on the Jakarta exchange. "It's the first time this has ever happened in my 20 years in the stock market," said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at stockbroker Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia. MSCI's move seemed heavy-handed given the steps Indonesia has taken to [USN:L6N42W0D2 TEXT:"address issues"] around market transparency and increase the free-float requirement for listed firms, Mackintosh said. "The only way for Indonesia to remedy this situation would be to impose severe sanctions and fines on those involved in concerted share manipulation," he said. DOWNGRADE PLANNED FOR MID-2027 MSCI said it will run a consultation with market participants for a downgrade to "standalone" status until April 2027 and then proceed with reclassification unless it finds clear evidence of improvement in market governance and function. Standalone markets are not included in MSCI's emerging or frontier index products, which are tracked by passive funds and treated as performance benchmarks for other fund managers. MSCI says reclassification to standalone status may occur in the case of severe deterioration in market accessibility or size and liquidity, with the most recent example being Argentina. Indonesia, Southeast Asia's biggest economy, would be the largest market to be downgraded to that classification.

item.title: Investors temper Anthropic IPO valuation expectations over revenue growth slowdown, sources say
item.description: Some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming initial public offering are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, amid broader concerns over the ballooning cost of financing AI.
item.dc:creator: Milana Vinn, Anirban Sen
item.content:encoded: Some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming initial public offering are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, four people familiar with the matter said, amid broader concerns over the ballooning cost of financing AI. Some investors who attended [USN:L6N4601AA TEXT:"Anthropic's investor day"] on Wednesday in San Francisco discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, three of the people said, a significant step down from the roughly $2 trillion valuation that investors had previously expected for the November share sale. At Wednesday's meeting, Anthropic told prospective IPO investors that its third-quarter revenue jumped 45% to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter, and that it was profitable on an adjusted basis during the quarter. While those numbers assuaged some concerns about the massive costs of developing AI systems, some investors were disappointed by the slowing sequential growth rate in the latest quarter, as Anthropic's revenue more than doubled from the first quarter to $11.6 billion in the second quarter, the people added. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A cooler reception for Anthropic's IPO could weigh on the wider AI market, whose near-term prospects investors see as hinging largely on the share sale's success, followed by [USN:L6N45407M TEXT:"OpenAI's potential listing"] next year. BELLWETHER IPO The concerns from investors come as a tech selloff is roiling global financial markets and has hurt AI infrastructure companies, chipmakers and so-called neocloud providers that rent computing power for AI broadly. Shares and bonds of Nvidia (NVDA.O) -backed CoreWeave (CRWV.O) [USN:L4N46111C TEXT:" tumbled on Thursday"], reflecting growing investor concern about an AI buildout that is increasingly being financed with borrowed money. A disappointing share sale for Anthropic could further add to investor worries about the AI buildout. The IPO market has suffered [USN:L6N45H0SG TEXT:"some setbacks"] recently, after data center operator SB Energy decided to delay its listing last month, while nuclear technology company Holtec Nuclear [USN:L4N4581N0 TEXT:"pulled its plans to go public"]. During Wednesday's meeting at Anthropic's headquarters in San Francisco, attendees, mostly the company's most prominent investors, met with CEO Dario Amodei and finance chief Krishna Rao. The Information earlier reported that investors were considering a lower valuation. Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives including Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who is now Anthropic's president, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. The company's rapid growth has been underpinned by Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google and Amazon (AMZN.O) , which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors. Last year, Anthropic's revenue surged twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis, excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, Reuters [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"reported "]last month. In its IPO prospectus seen exclusively by Reuters in September, Anthropic laid out a vision that AI will transform the global economy more profoundly than industrialization, electricity and the internet, even as it reported a loss of $42 billion in 2025 and projected more spending for the upcoming AI buildout. The company has committed to spending [USN:L1N45K0RM TEXT:"at least $518 billion"] over a decade for cloud services, computing and infrastructure.

item.title: Volvo Cars expands automated driving partnership with Nvidia
item.description: The companies said Volvo would combine its safety systems and engineering expertise with Nvidia's artificial intelligence and computing technologies.
item.dc:creator: Marie Mannes
item.content:encoded: Volvo Cars (VOLCARb.ST) is expanding its partnership with Nvidia (NVDA.O) to [USN:L6N3Y610S TEXT:"develop"] a new generation of driver-assistance and automated-driving technology, the companies said on Thursday, as carmakers race to bring increasingly advanced hands-free driving features to market. The companies said Volvo would combine its safety systems and engineering expertise with Nvidia's artificial intelligence and computing technologies, including the Hyperion sensor, computer architecture and autonomous-driving software stack. Automakers including Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Ford have been targeting more advanced automated-driving systems, from hands-free highway driving to self-driving in limited conditions. Tesla is [USN:L6N45R0YL TEXT:"pushing"] for broader [USN:L6N45V0PF TEXT:"approval"] of its assisted-driving technology in Europe, including urban areas with an EU-wide [USN:L6N45H0TX TEXT:"vote"] possible in December. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told reporters in Stockholm that partnering with Volvo provided the chipmaker with a "tremendous opportunity" because of the automaker's rigorous safety standards. Huang said features would be rolled out gradually. "As the car earns its trust and as Volvo becomes comfortable with the capabilities of the cars, they'll continue to expand the services that are available. There's no hurry, safety first," Huang said. Besides Volvo, Nvidia has [USN:L1N3Y90FP TEXT:"partnerships"] with a wide range of automakers, including Mercedes, Jaguar Land Rover and Hyundai. Volvo CEO Hakan Samuelsson said the company would take a cautious approach to deployment. "We will never let it out under conditions which we know are not safe," Samuelsson told reporters. The technology, which Volvo ultimately expects to support hands-free driving both in urban environments and on highways, should appear in Volvo vehicles before 2030 and will be launched in multiple regions simultaneously, excluding China, Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo Cars' head of software engineering, said. Volvo, majority-owned by China's Geely Holding (GEELY.UL), has not chosen a pricing model yet, Bakkenes said, but features would not be limited to higher-priced models.

item.title: Infantino apology fails to sway England, Germany over FIFA future
item.description: Gianni Infantino apologised to the FIFA Council, but English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced he was fit to continue as president of soccer's world governing body.
item.dc:creator: Iain Axon
item.content:encoded: Gianni Infantino apologised to the FIFA Council on Thursday, but English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced he was fit to continue as president of soccer's world governing body. Infantino said he had apologised during the closed meeting for mistakes in communicating and consulting over the now-abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project, but stressed that it had been only a proposal and “in no way a done deal”. "First of all, I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, which then led to many consequences," Infantino said in a video published by FIFA. "But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal, so in no way a done deal." The FFE plan involved creating a company to run the commercial interests of FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and selling a minority stake to private investors. Infantino said it was intended to generate additional funding for FIFA’s 211 member associations. While Infantino appeared to retain strong support among African officials, opposition from some of Europe’s most influential football associations remained pronounced. German FA president Bernd Neuendorf called for a "complete restart" at FIFA, saying the governance reforms the organisation needed could not be delivered with Infantino in charge. "The first thing is we need reforms. That's true. And everyone knows that," Neuendorf said. "The old administration has to be reformed, and the whole governance has to be reformed. But I'm pretty clear here in this that this is not possible with Gianni. "So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart." English FA chair Debbie Hewitt said Infantino needed to provide answers to questions raised by FIFA Council members and warned that failure to do so would make him unfit to remain president. "I think the man has to answer those questions," Hewitt said. "And if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president." Neuendorf questioned the extent of Infantino’s apology, saying he believed it related primarily to the failure to consult the council rather than to the FFE project itself. "I didn't have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total," Neuendorf said. "My impression was it was just because it wasn't brought forward to the council and no one was involved." Neuendorf said council members had learned about the project through the media rather than from FIFA's leadership and that representatives from other confederations had also complained about the lack of consultation. "When it came to the FFE project as such, I have the impression that this still was not included when he apologised," he said. QUESTIONS UNANSWERED Hewitt said Infantino’s apparent regret over not consulting the council strengthened the case for releasing the relevant FFE documents to its members. "You have an obligation. We all have an obligation, a fiduciary responsibility to answer the questions that have been put forward," Hewitt said. "He told us to submit those questions. There were so many of them, and now it's up to him to do that and do that in the open way. "If there's nothing to hide, then share (the FFE documents) with us... if you regret it that deeply, please share it with us." The meeting also dealt with calls for reform at FIFA, but Hewitt said meaningful changes could not be made until members understood how the decisions at the centre of recent controversies had been reached. She cited FFE, the decision to suspend the automatic one-match ban imposed on United States forward Folarin Balogun after his World Cup red card, and the FIFA Peace Prize awarded to US President Donald Trump as issues requiring greater scrutiny. "Unless we understand what happened, either it was a massive failing in governance because it wasn't followed or actually the governance was followed, but there was something else that got to what we all felt in there was the wrong decisions," Hewitt said. "So we must understand what happened in order to be able to review it. Otherwise we're guessing." The criticism, however, was not unanimous. Ahmed Yahya, the president of the Football Federation of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania (FFRIM), defended Infantino, saying his leadership had helped develop football around the world, pointing to increased funding for national associations and the expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams. "We (the African nations) believe Gianni is the right person to continue leading football," Yahya said. Asked whether most people wanted Infantino to remain president, he added: "I'm certain. The majority want Gianni to stay."

item.title: UBS exploring options abroad in case Swiss rules prove intolerable, sources say
item.description: UBS is working on possible scenarios including shifting its headquarters, or a merger with another bank, if Switzerland introduces new banking rules it deems excessively strict, according to three people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Hirt
item.content:encoded: UBS is working on possible scenarios including shifting its headquarters, or a merger with another bank, if Switzerland introduces new banking rules it deems excessively strict, according to three people familiar with the matter. Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse, and a lower house committee will later this month begin debating rules [USN:L8N45F0DE TEXT:"passed"] in September by the upper house that UBS hinted were intolerable. A group inside the bank is considering the various options, which include drawing up a list of smaller banks in the United States that UBS could potentially buy, and the prospect of the bank being taken over itself, according to the sources. There are no active talks underway, the sources said. UBS, which is closely following how events play out in parliament, said: "We don't comment on speculation or views expressed on such matters." The British government and UBS discussed this year the possibility of a move to London if the bank were to redomicile, the Financial Times [USN:L6N46207S TEXT:"said"] on Friday. The city [USN:L8N3SK1LO TEXT:"emerged"] as one of the best options in the bank's 2025 contingency planning, a source told Reuters at the time. In March, UBS obtained a US banking licence and is eager to expand its business in the United States. But the rules drafted by the Swiss government are partly designed to reduce the risk taxpayers could face if the bank suffered losses in the United States. People familiar with the bank's thinking say US investment bank Morgan Stanley (MS.N) would be the best theoretical match for UBS. The Swiss bank has repeatedly stated that it is not planning to move and sees great value in its Swiss base. There are notable ties between the leadership of the two banks, as UBS Chairman Colm Kelleher spent many years at Morgan Stanley, eventually rising to one of the top jobs there. Kelleher said last month that UBS might need to [USN:L8N4590WE TEXT:"consider"] its future in Switzerland if the incoming rules were too harsh. Under its overhaul, the Swiss government wants UBS to back its foreign units with 100% Common Equity Tier 1 capital, which could tie up in excess of $20 billion. UBS views this as excessive and harmful to its international competitiveness. The upper house last month trimmed that requirement to 90% CET1 capital, but UBS also regards that as excessively high. At present, the bank needs to 60% capitalise its foreign units but that can be partly met with cheaper capital. Since last year, speculation has swirled around the possibility that UBS could move its base abroad to avoid the tougher regulation, and people familiar with the bank's thinking say it has a duty to shareholders to consider all options. Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who has led the charge to introduce tougher banking rules, said last month she felt it was unlikely that UBS would leave its homeland, arguing this would be costly and legally complicated.

item.title: How are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?
item.description: Houthi militants who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week attacked Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door.
item.dc:creator: John Davison
item.content:encoded: Houthi [USN:L6N4010N9 TEXT:"militants"] who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week [USN:L6N4600NM TEXT:"attacked"] Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door. The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe [USN:L6N4600CJ TEXT:"international investment hub"] as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil. This nightmare scenario for a key US ally in the Gulf has been years in the making, weapons and regional experts say. They attribute [USN:L1N46108L TEXT:"Saudi Arabia's vulnerability"] to a perfect storm of factors that include Tehran helping the Houthis reach near self-sufficiency in producing and deploying advanced weapons, bolstering the ragtag Yemeni group, and the impact of the US war on Iran, which has depleted stocks of interceptors. TRAINING TO SELF-SUFFICIENCY BY IRAN Iran has been giving [USN:L1N43P0D6 TEXT:"weapons, money and training"] to the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade, although Tehran has officially denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN arms embargo. While Iran has come under its own financial and military strains due to war and sanctions, the Houthis have learned – with Iranian help – how to assemble their own weapons, including drones and missiles, the experts interviewed by Reuters said. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and members of Iran's other ally, Lebanese Hezbollah, initially gave the Houthis knowledge of missile systems and their operation, said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London. "Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities," he said. "Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted." Iranian analysts said that the Houthis have in this way become one of the most cost-effective and valuable military proxies of Iran. "The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn't receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces," said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Nikou said this strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles. "Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish," Nikou said. The Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a number of missiles fired by the Houthis at Saudi cities, and that it has destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms. Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki [USN:L1N4610M8 TEXT:"told a press conference"] the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats. DIVERSIFYING WEAPONS IMPORTS AND TECHNOLOGY A key strength of the Houthis in building their own weapons is that they don't rely solely on Iranian-made equipment or imports coming from Iran. The Conflict Armament Research organization said in a report this week that the Houthis were attempting to make advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using parts shipped from China, after Yemen's internationally recognised government seized one such shipment. "China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially," Krieg said. The Houthis have also experimented with artificial intelligence in efforts to improve their weapons' effectiveness. Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle. WAR FATIGUE, DEPLETED MUNITIONS While the Houthis have improved their weapons production, US allies in the region have seen their air defences stretched since the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. The United States has used large amounts of the missile interceptors it deploys in the region to protect its bases and its allies, which include Israel and Gulf countries, leaving some vulnerable, Saudi Arabia in particular. "Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do," said Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute. Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defence against air attacks harder than defending Israel or a US base, he said. WAR EXPERIENCE The Houthis have learned from the increased levels of violence in the region in recent years, Sabet said. A Yemeni civil war, in which the Houthis battled Saudi-backed forces from 2014, settled into a shaky ceasefire in 2022. But after Israel’s assault on Gaza in 2023 , which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting shipping through the Red Sea. The fallout from the US-Iran war this year reignited the Yemeni civil war, by which time the Houthis had developed new capabilities. "They haven't been sitting still," Sabet said. "They were basically diversifying their supply chains... and as they gain operational experience, they're able to make those weapons more sophisticated."

item.title: Tesla's new Roadster turns in air with SpaceX thrusters, won't land until 2028
item.description: Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.
item.dc:creator: Abhirup Roy, Mrinmay Dey
item.content:encoded: Tesla (TSLA.O) unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters on Thursday and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car. The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters. Later in the event it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the maneuver. Some watchers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two big companies he controls, an idea he has explored by discussing their overlap. The reveal gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics, and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors. "It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers," Gene Munster, managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on social media platform X. "The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can't wait to bring (Tesla) and (SpaceX) together," Munster said. Musk has played down the car's importance to Tesla's finances, describing it in 2023 as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially." But the car still carries symbolic weight. "Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker's best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla's new halo car," Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month. Viewers and witnesses gushed over the spectacle of the launch. "That was the most insane product demo I've ever seen," Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. "I just saw this in person, and I'm still asking how this wasn't AI." Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at Thursday's event, although Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of $200,000 for the vehicle. Tesla's reservation page for the Roadster after Thursday's event showed a "Performance" version of the vehicle requiring a $50,000 deposit and a "Thrust" version with "acceleration thrusters" requiring a $250,000 deposit. A "Rocket" variant, which Tesla says is "invite only," is described as a single-seat model with a "full flight system." 'HALFWAY TO THE SPEED OF SOUND' The event at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, had all the elements of a classic Musk product reveal: dramatic music, smoke, mechanical hissing sounds and a launch countdown. "This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers working closely together to make something that you haven't seen in any movie," Musk, wearing a silver Western-style belt buckle emblazoned with the Tesla logo, told a cheering crowd of enthusiasts and investors. The Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 mph (97 kph) in less than one second and can hit a top speed of over 230 mph (370 kph), Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said. "Definitely much faster than that," an excited Musk said. "I think you've got to crack halfway to the speed of sound." The Roadster can also travel over 300 miles (480 km) on a single charge. That is less than half of what Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla first revealed a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said that deliveries would begin in 2020. The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever electric vehicle and used a Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world's view of what an EV could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans. The reveal of the second-generation Roadster comes amid a sharp shift in Tesla's focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and robotics, from manufacturing cars for human drivers. This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab — a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors. Tesla is set to report third-quarter results on October 21. Sales of Tesla's aging lineup of EVs have declined over the past two years, although high gas prices helped boost deliveries in the third quarter. "The margin and cash flow numbers will carry far more weight with investors than anything they saw at the reveal," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at trading platform eToro.

item.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Zelenskiy says 'we're done' with Trump's energy truce
item.description: Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump, and criticised Trump's willingness to strike deals with Moscow. By effectively walking away from Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and openly criticising the US leader, Zelenskiy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia's refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said on Telegram that a [USN:S8N44O03I TEXT:"major Ukrainian drone attack"] had caused a fire at the refinery. Russian President Vladimir Putin [USN:L1N4610T1 TEXT:"played down"] the effect of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused "nothing particularly significant." After Trump's surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites, Kyiv suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. Zelenskiy's relations with Trump have been testy, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting descended into a shouting match. Zelenskiy has since praised Trump and US help for Ukraine, and in recent days said Ukraine fully backed the energy ceasefire despite waves of Russian attacks. PATIENCE RAN OUT In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," he told the newspaper. Zelenskiy also criticised what he saw as Trump's willingness to strike deals with Russia, apparent admiration for Putin and an affinity for those wielding power or considerable wealth. "He (Trump) speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people," the FT quoted him as saying. "Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong." In his comments to the FT, Zelenskiy also said he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX's Starlink receptors this week, which curbed Ukraine's ability to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," he told the FT. British Defence Minister Wes Streeting [USN:L1N46110U TEXT:"said on Thursday"] that he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine and called for both sides to "move forward in a collective spirit". "We need President Trump engaged on Ukraine. He has been, and the diplomatic track is as important in ending the war as making sure Ukraine has the weapons it needs to see off Russian aggression," he said on Fox News. EU SUMMIT Zelenskiy [USN:L1N46107Z TEXT:"was due to attend"] a European Union summit on Friday and in a series of meetings ahead of the gathering stressed the need to strengthen air defences. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump as president of the United States. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote. Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had "damn well better stop". Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Ukrainian officials say that for several days they have not received the usual warnings, which rely on US satellite detectors, from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles,. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials say that is too slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. Defence experts said, and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, meanwhile, [USN:L8N4601YV TEXT:"showed that"] Russia had in just six weeks nearly finished building a major base in southern Russia for launching jet-powered drones. Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump is under pressure to lower fuel prices, with his Republicans facing midterm elections in less than three weeks,. Prices for diesel have reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, though Trump says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. In the Black Sea, rescuers searched for seven missing sailors after [USN:L8N4610EC TEXT:"drones struck"] two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze in the latest attack on shipping along a vital route used by Ukraine. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was ongoing to do so.

item.title: US considers removing sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels to cut freight rates, official says
item.description: The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Gardner, Jarrett Renshaw
item.content:encoded: The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday. The discussions come days after President Donald Trump temporarily [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"lifted sanctions"] on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, [USN:S8N43U03J TEXT:"European"] countries and some of Trump's [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"fellow Republicans"] in the US Senate. Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine. The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures. The goal is to move more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said. Companies seeking to buy the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department for approval of the transactions, the official said. A Treasury Department official told Reuters that the agency undertakes a "thorough review before removing sanctions on any entity." If legitimate buyers want to purchase the vessels and restore them for use by global commercial shipping, Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control "may consider authorizing those transactions and removing sanctions on those vessels on a case-by-case basis," the official said. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was discussing easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to lower record freight rates that have hurt demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group. Portions of the remarks were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available. The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia move oil or oil products. But Trump's push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels. The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment. High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7. RECORD HIGHS Tanker freight rates have [USN:L4N45U0OZ TEXT:"soared to record highs"] as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America. Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East. Lifting the sanctions on the tankers, which are mostly old and not well maintained, is "unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months," it said in the note. Easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs," in the waterway between Iran and Oman. Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said.

item.title: Europe's battery boom has a dirty secret
item.description: Europe's battery boom is proving that storage can help lower peak power prices. But unless government policy changes, battery systems may simply profit from fossil-fuel use instead of helping to eliminate it.
item.dc:creator: Martin Vladimirov
item.content:encoded: Europe's battery boom is proving that storage can help lower peak power prices. But unless government policy changes, battery systems may simply profit from fossil-fuel use instead of helping to eliminate it. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) have proliferated in recent years, reshaping how profits are shared in the electricity market. Global storage capacity grew 66% last year to almost 302 gigawatts (GW), up 150-fold in a decade. Falling production costs are changing batteries from expensive renewable add-ons into game changers that are revolutionizing the structure of the power market. [USN:L6N42U0QP TEXT:"Europe is a"] case in point. The continent installed 36 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage last year, bringing its total above 100 GWh, a tenfold rise, according to SolarPower Europe , which expects additions to exceed 50 GWh in 2026. Much of that investment remains concentrated in a few markets, led by Germany, Bulgaria and Italy. While natural gas benchmarks still largely determine European power prices, battery systems in those markets are quickly eroding that dominance. That’s because batteries are — in power industry terms — cutting the head off “the duck”. The so-called "duck curve" describes the typical pattern for European power prices. They usually fall to zero or below during sunny hours as surplus solar power floods the market, then rise with evening demand as fossil-fuel plants, mostly coal- and gas-powered, replace photovoltaic (PV) output. Increasingly, batteries are absorbing surplus electricity during peak PV production – so buying power when it’s cheap – and then discharging it during evening hours when it can fetch a much higher price. This flattens the price curve, as battery systems profit handsomely from decapitating the “duck”. And profit they do. European carbon costs make electricity prices in those evening hours – when most of the power is still coming from fossil fuels – particularly expensive. This has been amplified this year by soaring gas prices related to the Iran war -driven global energy squeeze. For example, in Bulgaria, where batteries account for more than 20% of installed generation capacity, one of the world's highest storage shares, BESS can now capture spreads exceeding €100 per megawatt-hour (MWh) based on data analysis from the Bulgarian power exchange, IBEX. Consumers have benefited as well. Bulgarian power prices have already fallen around 15% relative to neighbouring markets over the last six months. Battery systems have made more electricity available during what are usually the most expensive evening hours, according to data from Bulgaria's transmission system operator. Bulgaria is not alone. Other European countries are experiencing similar price dynamics, including Spain, Portugal, Italy, Britain and Germany where batteries are absorbing surplus wind and solar electricity that would otherwise be curtailed by the grid operators. FOSSIL FUEL PARADOX BESS are expected to facilitate the energy transition, by reducing the volatility inherent in many renewables. But what the above spreads show is that, in many leading markets, battery systems are benefiting from the very fossil-fuel dependence they promise to eliminate. Meanwhile, European Union governments are propping up this system by quietly subsidising coal and gas through complicated power capacity mechanisms intended to maintain grid stability. These mechanisms keep fossil-fuel-powered plants running despite their uncompetitive pricing outside of evening hours or the coldest months. The EU last month approved Germany's 15-year, €35.2 billion capacity mechanism to guarantee grid stability and long-term security of supply. Moreover, Italy, where gas supplies roughly 38% of electricity, paid roughly €1.8 billion through its long-standing capacity mechanism in 2025. The country recorded some of Europe's highest power prices last year. From a political perspective, these government efforts are understandable. Total grid decarbonisation may be the future goal, but European leaders may be loath to do anything today that could appear to threaten energy security, even if those risks may be overstated. The [USN:L6N3R70S7 TEXT:"blackout on the Iberian peninsula"] last year may not have been caused by renewables, but that didn't stop many from blaming them. WHAT’S NEXT? What other options might European leaders have? Scaling battery storage could potentially enable 24-hour green electricity. However, this would likely require governments to remunerate BESS operators for the critical role they’re playing in maintaining dependable, affordable energy. That’s because the spread of battery systems – and the elimination of the lucrative fossil-fuel window – would likely erode BESS margins substantially. Technical improvements would also be needed. Many battery systems store only two to three hours of full-power output. This requires European grids to adopt still prohibitively expensive long-duration energy storage (LDES) technologies — such as iron-air or redox flow batteries — that can discharge continuously for 10 to 100+ hours to manage multi-day grid imbalances. But even the most advanced batteries will not be able to sustain solar-heavy systems through prolonged winter lulls. This strengthens the case for diversified renewables, including wind that operates overnight and often produces more power in the winter. Battery storage is likely to anchor the energy transformation and the eventual phasing out of fossil fuels, but, for now, it’s profiting from their survival. Whether batteries can deliver the energy transition they are promising will be a matter of political will to overcome the vested fossil fuel interests. (The views expressed here are those of Martin Vladimirov , Director of the Geoeconomics Program of the Center for the Study of Democracy (CSD)) Enjoying this column? item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: L'Europe dans le vert, les craintes sur le secteur technologique s'apaisent
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Europe dans le vert, les craintes sur le secteur technologique s'apaisent PARIS, 16 octobre (Reuters) - Les principales Bourses européennes sont orientées dans le vert vendredi avec la stabilisation des rendements obligataires, ainsi que le reflux des cours pétroliers et de l'or après le choc provoqué par le spécialiste de l'intelligence artificielle (IA) CoreWeave. UniCredit autorisé par la BCE à prendre le contrôle de Commerzbank MILAN, 15 octobre (Reuters) - UniCredit a obtenu l'autorisation de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE) pour prendre le contrôle de Commerzbank, a annoncé jeudi soir la banque italienne, alors que son offre publique d'achat hostile a porté sa participation dans son concurrent allemand à 48%. UBS étudie des options à l'étranger au cas la réglementation suisse devient insupportable à ses yeux selon des sources ZURICH, 16 octobre (Reuters) - UBS étudie différents scénarios, dont un déménagement de son siège social ou une fusion avec une autre banque, au cas où la Suisse adopterait de nouvelles règles bancaires que le groupe jugerait excessivement strictes, selon trois sources proches du dossier. Schneider relève ses objectifs 2026 après un T3 record porté par les centres de données 16 octobre (Reuters) - Schneider Electric a relevé vendredi pour la deuxième fois de l’année ses objectifs de résultat d'exploitation et de chiffre d’affaires 2026, porté par la demande des géants du cloud pour les centres de données dédiés à l’intelligence artificielle. Christine Lagarde pourrait être nommée présidente du Forum de Davos dès novembre-sources ZURICH/BANGKOK, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le Forum économique mondial (WEF) pourrait nommer Christine Lagarde à sa présidence dès novembre, ont déclaré à Reuters quatre sources proches de l'organisation, ce qui impliquerait un départ anticipé de ses fonctions à la tête de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE). L’AIE va accélérer la mise sur le marché des stocks de pétrole, dont plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel PARIS, 15 octobre (Reuters) - L’Agence internationale de l’énergie (AIE) est convenue jeudi de mettre sur le marché plus de 20 millions de barils de diesel dès que possible, ainsi que les volumes restants des réserves d’urgence libérées en mars, afin de contribuer à approvisionner le marché et à freiner la flambée des prix. États-Unis: Les prix à la production enregistrent en septembre leur plus forte hausse en quatre ans et demi 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les prix à la production (PPI) aux États-Unis ont enregistré en septembre leur plus forte hausse en quatre ans et demi, sous l'effet de l'augmentation des coûts des biens et des services, dernier signe en date d'un élargissement des pressions inflationnistes au-delà des produits énergétiques. États-Unis: Les ventes au détail augmentent plus que prévu en septembre avec les prix de l'essence WASHINGTON, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les ventes au détail aux Etats-Unis ont augmenté plus que prévu en septembre, portées par la hausse des prix de l'essence, même si les dépenses dans d'autres secteurs sont restées modérées, montrent les données publiées jeudi par le département du Commerce. Alstom prolonge de 15 ans son contrat avec Greater Anglia pour 800 millions de livres sterling 15 octobre (Reuters) - Alstom a annoncé jeudi avoir signé une prolongation de 15 ans de son contrat de maintenance avec l’opérateur ferroviaire britannique Greater Anglia, pour un montant d’environ 800 millions de livres sterling (946,38 millions d'euros). États-Unis: Hausse des inscriptions au chômage à 199.000 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les inscriptions au chômage ont augmenté aux États-Unis, s'établissant à 199.000 lors de la semaine au 10 octobre, a annoncé jeudi le département du Travail.

item.content:encoded: USA: Une fusillade dans une école de l'Oregon fait quatre morts, le tireur abattu 15 octobre (Reuters) - Un adolescent de 16 ans a ouvert le feu jeudi dans une école primaire de Bend, dans l'Oregon, faisant quatre morts, dont trois enfants, avant d'être abattu par une personne qui l'avait poursuivi dans l'établissement, a annoncé la police. La Chine est prête à coopérer avec l'UE pour remédier aux déséquilibres mondiaux PÉKIN, 16 octobre (Reuters) - La Chine est prête à engager un dialogue avec l'Union européenne (UE) pour améliorer la communication sur certains aspects de la gouvernance économique mondiale et de la coordination des politiques macroéconomiques, a déclaré vendredi le ministre chinois des Finances. La reprise des frappes ukrainiennes contre les raffineries russes est une "honte", dit Trump 16 octobre (Reuters) - La reprise des frappes ukrainiennes contre les raffineries russes est une "honte" qui maintient les prix mondiaux de l'énergie à un niveau élevé, a déclaré le président américain Donald Trump à la chaîne Newsmax lors d'une interview diffusée jeudi. Ukraine : La décision de limiter le réseau Starshield a été prise à la Maison blanche selon des sources NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'ordre de limiter l'utilisation du réseau de satellites à usage militaire Starshield, développé par SpaceX, utilisé par l'Ukraine est venu de la Maison blanche, selon deux responsables américains et un responsable occidental au fait de la question. Lula promet la gratuité des transports en commun le week-end BRASILIA, 16 octobre (Reuters) - Le président brésilien Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a déclaré jeudi qu'il allait soumettre au Parlement un amendement constitutionnel garantissant la gratuité des transports publics le week-end, une nouvelle mesure à destination des revenus modestes avant le deuxième tour de l'élection présidentielle. La nouvelle porte-parole de la Maison Blanche admet avoir échoué l'examen du barreau WASHINGTON, 16 octobre (Reuters) - La nouvelle porte-parole de la Maison blanche, Katie Zacharia, a déclaré jeudi soir qu'elle n'avait pas réussi l'examen du barreau, ce qui, selon la plupart des experts juridiques, lui interdit de prétendre au titre d'avocate alors qu'elle s'est initialement présentée comme telle. États-Unis/Midterms: Des enquêtes sur l'empire Trump se profilent au Congrès WASHINGTON, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Les contributeurs à la construction de la salle de bal du président américain Donald Trump et les partenaires impliqués dans des opérations conclues par des membres de sa famille devraient figurer parmi les premières cibles d'enquêtes si les démocrates reprennent le contrôle de la Chambre des représentants ou du Sénat lors des élections de mi-mandat de novembre, selon plusieurs sources parlementaires et juridiques. Yémen: Explosions près du palais présidentiel à Aden, attaqué par les Houthis 15 octobre (Reuters) - Deux officiers de sécurité ont été tués jeudi au Yémen dans une attaque au missile contre le palais présidentiel à Aden, dans le sud du pays, ont déclaré à Reuters deux représentants du gouvernement, rapportant que les Houthis avaient tiré plusieurs missiles en direction du bâtiment. L'exécution de l'auteur de la fusillade de Ford Hood ne sera pas diffusée en direct, dit Trump WASHINGTON, 15 octobre (Reuters) - - Le président américain Donald Trump a déclaré jeudi que l'exécution de Nidal Hasan, condamné à mort pour le meurtre de 13 personnes sur la base militaire de Fort Hood au Texas en 2009, ne serait finalement pas diffusée en direct. Le sommet UE-Golfe prévu le 24/10 à Ryad est reporté RYAD/BRUXELLES, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le sommet prévu le 24 octobre à Ryad entre l'Union européenne et le Conseil de coopération du Golfe (CCG) a été reporté jeudi pour des raisons de sécurité, en raison notamment des attaques répétées des Houthis contre l'Arabie saoudite qui perturbent le trafic aérien.
